definition: Astute means very clever and perceptive.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word astute. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know astute should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: An astute floor nurse noticed that the fevers spiked only on delivery days, and traced the outbreak to a contaminated ice machine.

Observant is the entry level — the changed haircut, the new lock, the side street all get noticed, with no guess yet about what they mean. Observant is milder than astute, which works out what all that noticing adds up to.
Prophetic goes further than astute — the astute reader works out what the clues on the table mean; a prophetic one would need cards nobody has dealt yet.

Perceptive credits the seeing-through: you register what is really going on beneath the surface — the forced smile, the deal quietly souring. Astute goes a step further, into action: reading the signs correctly and knowing what to do about them. A perceptive friend notices you are upset; an astute one knows what will help.

Sharp-eyed praises the eyes alone: no detail escapes — the smudged signature, the moved chair — but it says nothing about understanding what the details mean. Astute is the full circuit, catching the tell and reading it right. A sharp-eyed proofreader finds every typo; an astute editor sees why the argument keeps failing.

Latin astus, 'cunning,' left no other everyday English word behind — astute is its lone descendant, so there is no cousin to peel out and reuse.
Astute means very clever and perceptive.
Ivanov needed one morning to read her new classroom.

She noticed that the twins traded a glance before every burst of laughter, and that the quiet boy by the window finished worksheets early and hid them — so by the second week the astute new teacher had split the twins and made the quiet boy her grader, heading off both the pranks and the boredom.
Astute is the right word because astute means very clever and perceptive — she reads small signs correctly and acts on the reading.
Observant alone would only say she noticed the glances; astute credits the inference, the step from noticing to knowing what it means.
Astute compliments the read — of people, markets, motives.
Its unit-mates split the territory: acumen is the seasoned judgment of a whole field, prudence the caution about risk, erudite the depth of book-learning.
Astute is for the sharp eye that catches today's tell and knows what it means.

With four minutes left and her team down nine, Coach Reyes noticed something small: the other team's center had stopped jumping for rebounds.
The star was gassed, and his teammates were covering for him by fouling.
An astute coach does two things with a detail like that -- reads it right, and turns it into a plan.
Reyes called the play her team had practiced but never used: drive at the center, again and again, until the fouls piled up.
He fouled out with ninety seconds left, and the nine-point lead went with him.
The scouts' report the next day used one word for Reyes, and it wasn't 'lucky.'
